title: voipred
text:
Computes the net benefit of using a model (treat if predicted risk is at or above the threshold), of treating everyone, and of treating no one, at each risk threshold, for a binary, survival or competing-risks outcome, for one model or several models validated on the same patients. This is the core quantity every other voipred validation metric (\(\Delta NB\), P(useful), P(best), EVPI, EVSI) is built on.

nb_val(
  data,
  predicted_risk = NULL,
  outcome,
  thresholds = seq(0, 0.99, by = 0.01),
  horizon = NULL,
  cause = NULL,
  cipcw = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  prior = nb_improper(),
  predict_function = NULL,
  label = NULL,
  subgroup = NULL,
  interval = NULL,
  n_sim = 1000
)





data


A data frame: the validation sample, one row per patient, with the outcome columns when outcome names them (and, for a fitted model, every covariate it uses; with cIPCW, every covariate of the censoring model).




predicted_risk


The predicted risks of the patients in data: a numeric vector, one probability per row of data (in its row order), e.g. val$p. Alternatively, the name of the column of data that holds them, e.g. “p”. For survival outcomes, the risk of the event by horizon (competing risks: of cause by horizon). This is all the validation needs. A fitted model can also be given instead: voipred predicts the risks from it (see "Predicting the risks from a model"). For several models: a list, each element a vector of risks, a column name or a fitted model, e.g. list(Full = fit1, Age = “p_age”) (see "Several models").




outcome


The observed outcome, one per row of data:


binary: a column name (“y”), a vector, or a one-sided formula (~ y); 0/1, logical (TRUE is the event) or a two-level factor (the event is level “1” if present, otherwise the second level);


survival: ~ Surv(time, status) (or a Surv object, or the name of a Surv column), with status 1 = event and 0 = censored;


competing risks: ~ Surv(time, status) where status is a factor whose first level is censoring and the other levels are the event types, e.g. factor(code, 0:2, c(“censored”, “relapse”, “death”)). Numeric codes 0/1/2 are not accepted (Surv() would turn 2 into NA).


Formulas are evaluated in data. Only right-censored outcomes are supported; missing or negative times and missing statuses are errors.




thresholds


Risk thresholds in [0, 1), in any order (kept as given). At threshold z a patient is treated when the predicted risk is >= z; a risk of exactly 0 is never treated.




horizon


Survival and competing-risks outcomes only (required there, an error for a binary outcome): the time by which the risk is predicted and the event counted, a single positive number in the units of the survival times. It must be within the follow-up of at least one patient.




cause


Competing-risks outcomes only: the event type of interest, one of the event levels of the outcome (default: the first event level). The net benefit is for "this cause by the horizon"; patients with another cause by then count as not having the event. The cause is passed to the model by its label, or by its position among the event levels if the model numbers its causes; so a model that numbers its causes must number them in the order of the outcome’s event levels.




cipcw


Survival and competing-risks outcomes only: how censoring is handled. NULL (default): Kaplan-Meier / Aalen-Johansen, which assumes censoring is independent of the outcome. To let censoring depend on covariates (conditional IPCW), give:


the covariates of the censoring, as a one-sided formula, e.g. cipcw = ~ age + nodes + grade: voipred fits coxph(Surv(time, censored) ~ age + nodes + grade) to the patients of data (with competing risks, only true censoring is censoring; with weights, weighted by them), predicts from it the probabilities of remaining uncensored, truncated at 0.02, and refits it in every draw of the value-of-information functions;


or your own censoring model fitted to the censoring times of data, e.g. cipcw = coxph(Surv(time, status == 0) ~ age, data = val);


or cipcw_control(), for more options: another truncation (cipcw_control(~ age + nodes, min_prob = 0.05), or min_prob = NULL for none), given weights, ties, or your own predict and refit functions for your censoring model.






weights


Optional case weights, one non-negative number per row of data (with a positive sum), e.g. sampling weights. They weight each patient in the net benefit (an integer weight is the same as repeating the row; 0 drops the patient), and the value-of-information functions then use the Bayesian bootstrap of the weighted sample. The Cox censoring model of cipcw = ~ covariates is fitted with them; they are not passed to the prediction model, nor to a censoring model you fitted yourself. Only with the improper prior.




prior


The prior (see "Prior" and nb_priors). Default nb_improper(): no prior information, the data only, which gives the usual net benefit. For a binary outcome, prior information can be added with nb_uniform(), nb_jeffreys(), your own Beta priors with nb_beta(), or nb_informative() (bayesDCA’s informative prior, whose sensitivity and specificity priors change with the threshold; for small effective sample sizes). Survival and competing-risks outcomes: only nb_improper().




predict_function


Optional, for fitted models only: a function(model, newdata, horizon, cause) that returns the predicted risks, used instead of the automatic routes (it always takes precedence). voipred calls it once with newdata = data; horizon and cause are those given to nb_val() (NULL when not used: horizon for a binary outcome, cause unless competing risks; cause is the event level’s label). It must return, in the row order of newdata, the probability of the event (binary), of the event by horizon (survival), or of cause by horizon (competing risks): either a vector, one column per outcome class (the event column is taken: “1” or “.pred_1”, otherwise the second of two), or a curve per patient, list(time = <grid>, surv = <n x grid matrix>) or list(time = <grid>, cif = <n x grid matrix>), read at the last grid time <= horizon. A function that ignores some arguments can be written function(model, newdata, …). With several fitted models, one function is used for each of them; or give a list of functions named by the labels of the models they are for, e.g. list(A = predict_a, B = predict_b) (the other models use the automatic routes). If voipred has no way to predict from a fitted model and no function is given for it, nb_val() stops before predicting, naming the models.




label


Optional names of the models in printed output and plots: a single string, or one per model, in order. Default: see "Labels".




subgroup


Optional subgroups, for the framework of Wang et al. on subgroup utility heterogeneity (see "Subgroups"): the name of a column of data, several column names (their combinations, e.g. c(“sex”, “smoker”)), or a factor or vector with one subgroup per row of data (factor levels keep their order; logical vectors give FALSE and TRUE). Every patient needs a subgroup; numeric variables with many values must be cut into categories first.




interval


Optional credible intervals: their level, a number between 0 and 1, e.g. 0.95 for 95% intervals. Default NULL: none (and no draws, so nb_val() is fast). With a level, nb_val() draws the net benefit n_sim times and keeps, at each threshold, the \((1 - level)/2\) and \((1 + level)/2\) quantiles of the draws of NB_model, NB_all and delta_NB (equal-tailed intervals). The draws are those of the value-of-information functions: for a binary outcome, the posterior (with the prior, e.g. nb_informative()); for survival and competing-risks outcomes, and with case weights, the Bayesian bootstrap (with cIPCW, refitting the censoring model in every draw, which takes longer). delta_NB is computed within each draw, so its interval follows the correlation of the model and treat all on the same patients. print(), summary() and as.data.frame() then show them, and plot(bands = TRUE) draws them as bands. The draws are random: call set.seed() first to reproduce them. Credible intervals show the uncertainty of each net benefit on its own, which is not a good measure of the uncertainty that matters for choosing a strategy, so nb_val() and every method that shows them warn and recommend value-of-information analysis (evpi(), with P(useful) and P(best)) instead.




n_sim


Number of draws for interval. Default 1000.



Binary outcome. With outcome \(Y\), predicted risk \(\hat\pi\) and threshold \(z\),


\(NB_{model}(z) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i Y_i T_i - \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (1-Y_i) T_i \frac{z}{1-z},\quad T_i = 1(\hat\pi_i \ge z)\)


\(NB_{all}(z) = \bar Y - (1-\bar Y)\frac{z}{1-z}, \qquad NB_{none}(z) = 0.\)
Survival outcome (Surv(time, status), with a horizon). The event is "the event by the horizon". With \(q\) the share treated at threshold \(z\) and \(F_+\) the risk of the event by the horizon among them, \(NB_{model} = q F_+ - q (1 - F_+) z/(1-z)\). Two estimators:


Kaplan-Meier (default, cipcw not given): \(F_+\) and the overall risk are Kaplan-Meier estimates (Aalen-Johansen for competing risks), as in dcurves. If none of the treated patients is followed up to the horizon, the net benefit at that threshold is NA, with a warning.


cIPCW, when cipcw is given: conditional inverse probability of censoring weighting, which allows censoring to depend on covariates. Patients with the event by the horizon are weighted by \(1/\hat G(T_i- \mid X_i)\), patients event-free at the horizon by \(1/\hat G(\tau \mid X_i)\), and patients censored before the horizon get no weight. The risk by the horizon is \(\sum_{events} w_i / n\); sensitivity and specificity are weighted proportions, and \(NB = \pi Se - (1-\pi)(1-Sp) z/(1-z)\). Usually cipcw is just the covariates of the censoring, e.g. cipcw = ~ age + nodes: voipred fits a Cox model of the censoring times of data on them and truncates the probabilities of remaining uncensored at 0.02 (weights at 50). See cipcw_control() for your own censoring model, given weights, or other truncation.


Competing risks (Surv(time, status) with a factor status whose first level is censoring). The event is cause (default: the first event level) by the horizon; a patient with a competing event by the horizon counts as not having the event. The model must predict the cumulative incidence of that cause; for competing risks only true censoring is censoring.
A patient is treated when the predicted risk is at or above the threshold, and a predicted risk of exactly 0 is never treated, as in dcurves.
Prior. nb_val() works in a Bayesian framework, which the value-of-information functions (evpi(), with P(useful) and P(best), and evsi()) use to represent the uncertainty of the net benefit. By default it uses no prior information: with the improper prior nb_improper() (Beta(0, 0)) only the data are used, and the net benefit is exactly the usual one, \(TP/n - FP/n \cdot z/(1-z)\). For a binary outcome, prior information can be added with another prior (nb_uniform(), nb_jeffreys(), your own with nb_beta(), or bayesDCA’s threshold-varying informative prior nb_informative(); see nb_priors): the prevalence \(\pi\) and, at each threshold, the sensitivity \(Se\) and specificity \(Sp\) of the model then have Beta priors, updated with the validation data (as in bayesDCA), and the net benefit columns are the posterior means, \(E[\pi] E[Se] - (1 - E[\pi])(1 - E[Sp]) z/(1-z)\) and \(E[\pi] - (1 - E[\pi]) z/(1-z)\). Survival and competing-risks outcomes use only the improper prior: their net benefit is the usual Kaplan-Meier, Aalen-Johansen or cIPCW estimate.
Predicted risks. Validation needs only the predicted risks of the patients in data: give them with predicted_risk, a numeric vector with one risk per row of data, e.g. predicted_risk = val$p. The name of the column of data that holds them works too: predicted_risk = “p” is the same as predicted_risk = val$p when data = val. The model object is not needed, and the risks can come from anywhere (an R model, published coefficients, other software). The outcome alone decides the type of analysis (binary, survival or competing risks).
Several models. To compare models, give them in one call as a list, each element one model: a vector of risks, the name of a column of data, or a fitted model, mixed freely, e.g. predicted_risk = list(Full = fit1, Age = “p_age”, Old = val$p_old). All are predicted for the same patients (the rows of data), and every other argument (outcome, thresholds, horizon, cause, cipcw, prior, weights) applies to all of them. (c() cannot hold several models: it joins vectors into one and takes fitted models apart, so voipred asks for list().) The result is the same as computing each model separately and combining the results with c(), and the value-of-information functions draw the models jointly, so their correlation on the same patients is kept. With cIPCW, one censoring model (and one set of censoring weights) is used for all the models. To compare a different set of models, call nb_val() with those models.
Labels. Each model is labelled, in printed output and plots, by the first of:


label, if given (one per model);


its name in the list, e.g. list(Full = …);


the column name, when it is given as one, e.g. “p_glm”;


the name in the call: of the object (p_glm, fit_glm), or after $ (val$p_glm gives p_glm);


otherwise “Model” (one model) or “Model 1”, “Model 2”, … (by position).


The labels must be different, and cannot be “Treat All” or “Treat None” (the default strategies); otherwise nb_val() stops and asks for names.
Subgroups. With subgroup, nb_val() also computes the net benefit of each model, treat all and treat none within each subgroup (Step 1 of the framework of Wang et al.), with the same estimator (with cIPCW, the censoring weights of the whole sample). When the incremental utility of a true positive relative to a false negative (\(a - c\), written \(k\)) differs between subgroups, population-level net benefit can favour a strategy that population utility does not favour. summary() checks this: whether the subgroup-specific differences in net benefit against a comparator have the same sign (Step 2: if they do, differences in \(k\) cannot change the population conclusion), the K-value for two subgroups (the critical ratio \(k_1/k_2\) at which the conclusion changes) and, with k (e.g. the relative risk reductions of the treatment in each subgroup, for a prognostic model), whether population net benefit and population utility favour different strategies (Step 3; for more than two subgroups, k can be ranges). plot(type = “subgroups”) draws the subgroup differences in net benefit, and plot(type = “region”) the inconsistency region of Wang et al. at one threshold. k_value() computes the K-value from published values. The result then has subgroups (the subgroups and their net benefit), and as.data.frame() has a subgroup column (“All” for the whole sample). Credible intervals are not available with subgroups.
Predicting the risks from a model (optional). Instead of the risks, the fitted model can be given as predicted_risk (e.g. nb_val(val, fit, “y”), or as an element of a list). voipred then predicts the risks of the patients in data from it, once, and every later step (the value-of-information functions, plots) reuses them: the probability of the event (binary), of the event by horizon (survival), or of cause by horizon (competing risks). There are two ways:


By default, from the model alone. voipred keeps no list of models: it uses predict() with type = “response” or type = “prob”, or riskRegression::predictRisk() (at horizon, and for cause), and its own prediction code only for models these get wrong. Checked in the tests against each package’s own predictions:


binary: glm (logit, probit, cloglog), logistf, mgcv::gam, earth, rpart, partykit::ctree, randomForest, ranger (probability = TRUE), gbm, xgboost, lightgbm, catboost, glmnet, cv.glmnet, e1071::svm (probability = TRUE), e1071::naiveBayes, naivebayes, nnet, MASS::lda, MASS::qda, kknn, and bayespred bpmfit and bpm (posterior mean of risk);


survival: coxph, rms::cph, survreg, rms::psm, flexsurvreg, flexsurvspline, rstpm2::stpm2, mgcv::gam with cox.ph(), ranger, randomForestSRC, aorsf, partykit::ctree, prodlim, and bayespred.dev Bayesian Cox and parametric survival models (posterior mean of risk);


competing risks: riskRegression::CSC, riskRegression::FGR (fitted for the requested cause), cmprsk::crr, competing-risks randomForestSRC, and survival’s multi-state coxph.


Any other model whose predict() returns probabilities in the usual way, or that has a riskRegression::predictRisk() method, works too. Models that only give relative risks or times (e.g. gbm and glmnet Cox models, rpart survival trees) have no route to probabilities. Before predicting, the covariates the model uses are compared with the columns of data, and missing ones are named in an error.


With predict_function, a function you write that returns the risks. It works for any model, and is the way to go when voipred stops with "Could not get predicted risks from this … model". If given, it is always used.


Whichever way they are given, the risks are checked: one per row, no NA, values in [0, 1] (log-odds, relative risks or predicted times are rejected as scores), and not only 0s and 1s (rejected as class labels). With a model, where the model’s own outcome can be read from its formula, voipred also stops or warns if it does not match outcome (e.g. a survival model with a binary outcome, or a binary model with a survival outcome), and warns if horizon is beyond the model’s own follow-up.
What voipred cannot check is the meaning of valid probabilities. With predict_function, make sure it returns the risk of the event (not the survival probability), by horizon and for cause.

An object of class voipred_nb, a list with:


estimates: a data frame with one row per model and threshold (by model, then threshold) and columns threshold, model (its label), NB_model (using the model; NA where it cannot be estimated, see Details), NB_all (treat everyone), NB_none (treat no one, always 0) and delta_NB, the difference in net benefit between the model and the best default strategy, \(NB_{model} - \max(NB_{all}, NB_{none})\): positive where the model is useful; net_FP_avoided, the net false positives avoided by the model compared with treat all (the net interventions avoided of Vickers and Elkin), \((NB_{model} - NB_{all}) / (t/(1-t))\): the gain in net benefit over treat all in units of false positives, e.g. 0.09 at \(t = 10\%\) is 9 unnecessary treatments avoided per 100 patients without missing more events (not defined at \(t = 0\)); with interval, also the bounds NB_model_lower, NB_model_upper, NB_all_lower, NB_all_upper, delta_NB_lower and delta_NB_upper, net_FP_avoided_lower, net_FP_avoided_upper;


interval (with interval): the level, n_sim and the kind of draws (“posterior” or “Bayesian bootstrap”);


models (the labels of the models), call and prior;


prior_shapes (binary outcome): the shapes \((a, b)\) of the Beta priors used at each threshold, for the sensitivity and specificity (se_a, se_b, sp_a, sp_b) and the prevalence (prev_a, prev_b): the same at every threshold, except for nb_informative();


outcome: the outcome type (“binary”, “survival” or “competing”), the number of patients n, the prevalence (binary: the posterior mean event rate; survival: the estimated risk of the event, or of cause, by the horizon), events (binary), and for survival outcomes horizon, cause and censoring (“km” or “cipcw”);


risk: the predicted risks, a matrix with one row per row of data and one column per model (named by its label);


counts (binary): the numbers of true and false positives and negatives of each model at each threshold;


observed, weights and cipcw: the outcome, case weights and censoring settings, used by the value-of-information functions.


Like a glm fit, it is a list whose parts are read with $ (e.g. res$estimates), and it has methods: print() shows what was evaluated and the first rows of estimates (several models: their net benefits side by side); summary() gives the best strategy, sensitivity and specificity at each threshold; plot() draws the decision curve or the \(\Delta NB\) curve of every model; as.data.frame() returns estimates; c() combines results.

title: voipred
text:
Computes the net benefit of using a model (treat if predicted risk is at or above the threshold), of treating everyone, and of treating no one, at each risk threshold, for a binary, survival or competing-risks outcome, for one model or several models validated on the same patients. This is the core quantity every other voipred validation metric (\(\Delta NB\), P(useful), P(best), EVPI, EVSI) is built on.

nb_val(
  data,
  predicted_risk = NULL,
  outcome,
  thresholds = seq(0, 0.99, by = 0.01),
  horizon = NULL,
  cause = NULL,
  cipcw = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  prior = nb_improper(),
  predict_function = NULL,
  label = NULL,
  subgroup = NULL,
  interval = NULL,
  n_sim = 1000
)





data


A data frame: the validation sample, one row per patient, with the outcome columns when outcome names them (and, for a fitted model, every covariate it uses; with cIPCW, every covariate of the censoring model).




predicted_risk


The predicted risks of the patients in data: a numeric vector, one probability per row of data (in its row order), e.g. val$p. Alternatively, the name of the column of data that holds them, e.g. “p”. For survival outcomes, the risk of the event by horizon (competing risks: of cause by horizon). This is all the validation needs. A fitted model can also be given instead: voipred predicts the risks from it (see "Predicting the risks from a model"). For several models: a list, each element a vector of risks, a column name or a fitted model, e.g. list(Full = fit1, Age = “p_age”) (see "Several models").




outcome


The observed outcome, one per row of data:


binary: a column name (“y”), a vector, or a one-sided formula (~ y); 0/1, logical (TRUE is the event) or a two-level factor (the event is level “1” if present, otherwise the second level);


survival: ~ Surv(time, status) (or a Surv object, or the name of a Surv column), with status 1 = event and 0 = censored;


competing risks: ~ Surv(time, status) where status is a factor whose first level is censoring and the other levels are the event types, e.g. factor(code, 0:2, c(“censored”, “relapse”, “death”)). Numeric codes 0/1/2 are not accepted (Surv() would turn 2 into NA).


Formulas are evaluated in data. Only right-censored outcomes are supported; missing or negative times and missing statuses are errors.




thresholds


Risk thresholds in [0, 1), in any order (kept as given). At threshold z a patient is treated when the predicted risk is >= z; a risk of exactly 0 is never treated.




horizon


Survival and competing-risks outcomes only (required there, an error for a binary outcome): the time by which the risk is predicted and the event counted, a single positive number in the units of the survival times. It must be within the follow-up of at least one patient.




cause


Competing-risks outcomes only: the event type of interest, one of the event levels of the outcome (default: the first event level). The net benefit is for "this cause by the horizon"; patients with another cause by then count as not having the event. The cause is passed to the model by its label, or by its position among the event levels if the model numbers its causes; so a model that numbers its causes must number them in the order of the outcome’s event levels.




cipcw


Survival and competing-risks outcomes only: how censoring is handled. NULL (default): Kaplan-Meier / Aalen-Johansen, which assumes censoring is independent of the outcome. To let censoring depend on covariates (conditional IPCW), give:


the covariates of the censoring, as a one-sided formula, e.g. cipcw = ~ age + nodes + grade: voipred fits coxph(Surv(time, censored) ~ age + nodes + grade) to the patients of data (with competing risks, only true censoring is censoring; with weights, weighted by them), predicts from it the probabilities of remaining uncensored, truncated at 0.02, and refits it in every draw of the value-of-information functions;


or your own censoring model fitted to the censoring times of data, e.g. cipcw = coxph(Surv(time, status == 0) ~ age, data = val);


or cipcw_control(), for more options: another truncation (cipcw_control(~ age + nodes, min_prob = 0.05), or min_prob = NULL for none), given weights, ties, or your own predict and refit functions for your censoring model.






weights


Optional case weights, one non-negative number per row of data (with a positive sum), e.g. sampling weights. They weight each patient in the net benefit (an integer weight is the same as repeating the row; 0 drops the patient), and the value-of-information functions then use the Bayesian bootstrap of the weighted sample. The Cox censoring model of cipcw = ~ covariates is fitted with them; they are not passed to the prediction model, nor to a censoring model you fitted yourself. Only with the improper prior.




prior


The prior (see "Prior" and nb_priors). Default nb_improper(): no prior information, the data only, which gives the usual net benefit. For a binary outcome, prior information can be added with nb_uniform(), nb_jeffreys(), your own Beta priors with nb_beta(), or nb_informative() (bayesDCA’s informative prior, whose sensitivity and specificity priors change with the threshold; for small effective sample sizes). Survival and competing-risks outcomes: only nb_improper().




predict_function


Optional, for fitted models only: a function(model, newdata, horizon, cause) that returns the predicted risks, used instead of the automatic routes (it always takes precedence). voipred calls it once with newdata = data; horizon and cause are those given to nb_val() (NULL when not used: horizon for a binary outcome, cause unless competing risks; cause is the event level’s label). It must return, in the row order of newdata, the probability of the event (binary), of the event by horizon (survival), or of cause by horizon (competing risks): either a vector, one column per outcome class (the event column is taken: “1” or “.pred_1”, otherwise the second of two), or a curve per patient, list(time = <grid>, surv = <n x grid matrix>) or list(time = <grid>, cif = <n x grid matrix>), read at the last grid time <= horizon. A function that ignores some arguments can be written function(model, newdata, …). With several fitted models, one function is used for each of them; or give a list of functions named by the labels of the models they are for, e.g. list(A = predict_a, B = predict_b) (the other models use the automatic routes). If voipred has no way to predict from a fitted model and no function is given for it, nb_val() stops before predicting, naming the models.




label


Optional names of the models in printed output and plots: a single string, or one per model, in order. Default: see "Labels".




subgroup


Optional subgroups, for the framework of Wang et al. on subgroup utility heterogeneity (see "Subgroups"): the name of a column of data, several column names (their combinations, e.g. c(“sex”, “smoker”)), or a factor or vector with one subgroup per row of data (factor levels keep their order; logical vectors give FALSE and TRUE). Every patient needs a subgroup; numeric variables with many values must be cut into categories first.




interval


Optional credible intervals: their level, a number between 0 and 1, e.g. 0.95 for 95% intervals. Default NULL: none (and no draws, so nb_val() is fast). With a level, nb_val() draws the net benefit n_sim times and keeps, at each threshold, the \((1 - level)/2\) and \((1 + level)/2\) quantiles of the draws of NB_model, NB_all and delta_NB (equal-tailed intervals). The draws are those of the value-of-information functions: for a binary outcome, the posterior (with the prior, e.g. nb_informative()); for survival and competing-risks outcomes, and with case weights, the Bayesian bootstrap (with cIPCW, refitting the censoring model in every draw, which takes longer). delta_NB is computed within each draw, so its interval follows the correlation of the model and treat all on the same patients. print(), summary() and as.data.frame() then show them, and plot(bands = TRUE) draws them as bands. The draws are random: call set.seed() first to reproduce them. Credible intervals show the uncertainty of each net benefit on its own, which is not a good measure of the uncertainty that matters for choosing a strategy, so nb_val() and every method that shows them warn and recommend value-of-information analysis (evpi(), with P(useful) and P(best)) instead.




n_sim


Number of draws for interval. Default 1000.



Binary outcome. With outcome \(Y\), predicted risk \(\hat\pi\) and threshold \(z\),


\(NB_{model}(z) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i Y_i T_i - \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (1-Y_i) T_i \frac{z}{1-z},\quad T_i = 1(\hat\pi_i \ge z)\)


\(NB_{all}(z) = \bar Y - (1-\bar Y)\frac{z}{1-z}, \qquad NB_{none}(z) = 0.\)
Survival outcome (Surv(time, status), with a horizon). The event is "the event by the horizon". With \(q\) the share treated at threshold \(z\) and \(F_+\) the risk of the event by the horizon among them, \(NB_{model} = q F_+ - q (1 - F_+) z/(1-z)\). Two estimators:


Kaplan-Meier (default, cipcw not given): \(F_+\) and the overall risk are Kaplan-Meier estimates (Aalen-Johansen for competing risks), as in dcurves. If none of the treated patients is followed up to the horizon, the net benefit at that threshold is NA, with a warning.


cIPCW, when cipcw is given: conditional inverse probability of censoring weighting, which allows censoring to depend on covariates. Patients with the event by the horizon are weighted by \(1/\hat G(T_i- \mid X_i)\), patients event-free at the horizon by \(1/\hat G(\tau \mid X_i)\), and patients censored before the horizon get no weight. The risk by the horizon is \(\sum_{events} w_i / n\); sensitivity and specificity are weighted proportions, and \(NB = \pi Se - (1-\pi)(1-Sp) z/(1-z)\). Usually cipcw is just the covariates of the censoring, e.g. cipcw = ~ age + nodes: voipred fits a Cox model of the censoring times of data on them and truncates the probabilities of remaining uncensored at 0.02 (weights at 50). See cipcw_control() for your own censoring model, given weights, or other truncation.


Competing risks (Surv(time, status) with a factor status whose first level is censoring). The event is cause (default: the first event level) by the horizon; a patient with a competing event by the horizon counts as not having the event. The model must predict the cumulative incidence of that cause; for competing risks only true censoring is censoring.
A patient is treated when the predicted risk is at or above the threshold, and a predicted risk of exactly 0 is never treated, as in dcurves.
Prior. nb_val() works in a Bayesian framework, which the value-of-information functions (evpi(), with P(useful) and P(best), and evsi()) use to represent the uncertainty of the net benefit. By default it uses no prior information: with the improper prior nb_improper() (Beta(0, 0)) only the data are used, and the net benefit is exactly the usual one, \(TP/n - FP/n \cdot z/(1-z)\). For a binary outcome, prior information can be added with another prior (nb_uniform(), nb_jeffreys(), your own with nb_beta(), or bayesDCA’s threshold-varying informative prior nb_informative(); see nb_priors): the prevalence \(\pi\) and, at each threshold, the sensitivity \(Se\) and specificity \(Sp\) of the model then have Beta priors, updated with the validation data (as in bayesDCA), and the net benefit columns are the posterior means, \(E[\pi] E[Se] - (1 - E[\pi])(1 - E[Sp]) z/(1-z)\) and \(E[\pi] - (1 - E[\pi]) z/(1-z)\). Survival and competing-risks outcomes use only the improper prior: their net benefit is the usual Kaplan-Meier, Aalen-Johansen or cIPCW estimate.
Predicted risks. Validation needs only the predicted risks of the patients in data: give them with predicted_risk, a numeric vector with one risk per row of data, e.g. predicted_risk = val$p. The name of the column of data that holds them works too: predicted_risk = “p” is the same as predicted_risk = val$p when data = val. The model object is not needed, and the risks can come from anywhere (an R model, published coefficients, other software). The outcome alone decides the type of analysis (binary, survival or competing risks).
Several models. To compare models, give them in one call as a list, each element one model: a vector of risks, the name of a column of data, or a fitted model, mixed freely, e.g. predicted_risk = list(Full = fit1, Age = “p_age”, Old = val$p_old). All are predicted for the same patients (the rows of data), and every other argument (outcome, thresholds, horizon, cause, cipcw, prior, weights) applies to all of them. (c() cannot hold several models: it joins vectors into one and takes fitted models apart, so voipred asks for list().) The result is the same as computing each model separately and combining the results with c(), and the value-of-information functions draw the models jointly, so their correlation on the same patients is kept. With cIPCW, one censoring model (and one set of censoring weights) is used for all the models. To compare a different set of models, call nb_val() with those models.
Labels. Each model is labelled, in printed output and plots, by the first of:


label, if given (one per model);


its name in the list, e.g. list(Full = …);


the column name, when it is given as one, e.g. “p_glm”;


the name in the call: of the object (p_glm, fit_glm), or after $ (val$p_glm gives p_glm);


otherwise “Model” (one model) or “Model 1”, “Model 2”, … (by position).


The labels must be different, and cannot be “Treat All” or “Treat None” (the default strategies); otherwise nb_val() stops and asks for names.
Subgroups. With subgroup, nb_val() also computes the net benefit of each model, treat all and treat none within each subgroup (Step 1 of the framework of Wang et al.), with the same estimator (with cIPCW, the censoring weights of the whole sample). When the incremental utility of a true positive relative to a false negative (\(a - c\), written \(k\)) differs between subgroups, population-level net benefit can favour a strategy that population utility does not favour. summary() checks this: whether the subgroup-specific differences in net benefit against a comparator have the same sign (Step 2: if they do, differences in \(k\) cannot change the population conclusion), the K-value for two subgroups (the critical ratio \(k_1/k_2\) at which the conclusion changes) and, with k (e.g. the relative risk reductions of the treatment in each subgroup, for a prognostic model), whether population net benefit and population utility favour different strategies (Step 3; for more than two subgroups, k can be ranges). plot(type = “subgroups”) draws the subgroup differences in net benefit, and plot(type = “region”) the inconsistency region of Wang et al. at one threshold. k_value() computes the K-value from published values. The result then has subgroups (the subgroups and their net benefit), and as.data.frame() has a subgroup column (“All” for the whole sample). Credible intervals are not available with subgroups.
Predicting the risks from a model (optional). Instead of the risks, the fitted model can be given as predicted_risk (e.g. nb_val(val, fit, “y”), or as an element of a list). voipred then predicts the risks of the patients in data from it, once, and every later step (the value-of-information functions, plots) reuses them: the probability of the event (binary), of the event by horizon (survival), or of cause by horizon (competing risks). There are two ways:


By default, from the model alone. voipred keeps no list of models: it uses predict() with type = “response” or type = “prob”, or riskRegression::predictRisk() (at horizon, and for cause), and its own prediction code only for models these get wrong. Checked in the tests against each package’s own predictions:


binary: glm (logit, probit, cloglog), logistf, mgcv::gam, earth, rpart, partykit::ctree, randomForest, ranger (probability = TRUE), gbm, xgboost, lightgbm, catboost, glmnet, cv.glmnet, e1071::svm (probability = TRUE), e1071::naiveBayes, naivebayes, nnet, MASS::lda, MASS::qda, kknn, and bayespred bpmfit and bpm (posterior mean of risk);


survival: coxph, rms::cph, survreg, rms::psm, flexsurvreg, flexsurvspline, rstpm2::stpm2, mgcv::gam with cox.ph(), ranger, randomForestSRC, aorsf, partykit::ctree, prodlim, and bayespred.dev Bayesian Cox and parametric survival models (posterior mean of risk);


competing risks: riskRegression::CSC, riskRegression::FGR (fitted for the requested cause), cmprsk::crr, competing-risks randomForestSRC, and survival’s multi-state coxph.


Any other model whose predict() returns probabilities in the usual way, or that has a riskRegression::predictRisk() method, works too. Models that only give relative risks or times (e.g. gbm and glmnet Cox models, rpart survival trees) have no route to probabilities. Before predicting, the covariates the model uses are compared with the columns of data, and missing ones are named in an error.


With predict_function, a function you write that returns the risks. It works for any model, and is the way to go when voipred stops with "Could not get predicted risks from this … model". If given, it is always used.


Whichever way they are given, the risks are checked: one per row, no NA, values in [0, 1] (log-odds, relative risks or predicted times are rejected as scores), and not only 0s and 1s (rejected as class labels). With a model, where the model’s own outcome can be read from its formula, voipred also stops or warns if it does not match outcome (e.g. a survival model with a binary outcome, or a binary model with a survival outcome), and warns if horizon is beyond the model’s own follow-up.
What voipred cannot check is the meaning of valid probabilities. With predict_function, make sure it returns the risk of the event (not the survival probability), by horizon and for cause.

An object of class voipred_nb, a list with:


estimates: a data frame with one row per model and threshold (by model, then threshold) and columns threshold, model (its label), NB_model (using the model; NA where it cannot be estimated, see Details), NB_all (treat everyone), NB_none (treat no one, always 0) and delta_NB, the difference in net benefit between the model and the best default strategy, \(NB_{model} - \max(NB_{all}, NB_{none})\): positive where the model is useful; net_FP_avoided, the net false positives avoided by the model compared with treat all (the net interventions avoided of Vickers and Elkin), \((NB_{model} - NB_{all}) / (t/(1-t))\): the gain in net benefit over treat all in units of false positives, e.g. 0.09 at \(t = 10\%\) is 9 unnecessary treatments avoided per 100 patients without missing more events (not defined at \(t = 0\)); with interval, also the bounds NB_model_lower, NB_model_upper, NB_all_lower, NB_all_upper, delta_NB_lower and delta_NB_upper, net_FP_avoided_lower, net_FP_avoided_upper;


interval (with interval): the level, n_sim and the kind of draws (“posterior” or “Bayesian bootstrap”);


models (the labels of the models), call and prior;


prior_shapes (binary outcome): the shapes \((a, b)\) of the Beta priors used at each threshold, for the sensitivity and specificity (se_a, se_b, sp_a, sp_b) and the prevalence (prev_a, prev_b): the same at every threshold, except for nb_informative();


outcome: the outcome type (“binary”, “survival” or “competing”), the number of patients n, the prevalence (binary: the posterior mean event rate; survival: the estimated risk of the event, or of cause, by the horizon), events (binary), and for survival outcomes horizon, cause and censoring (“km” or “cipcw”);


risk: the predicted risks, a matrix with one row per row of data and one column per model (named by its label);


counts (binary): the numbers of true and false positives and negatives of each model at each threshold;


observed, weights and cipcw: the outcome, case weights and censoring settings, used by the value-of-information functions.


Like a glm fit, it is a list whose parts are read with $ (e.g. res$estimates), and it has methods: print() shows what was evaluated and the first rows of estimates (several models: their net benefits side by side); summary() gives the best strategy, sensitivity and specificity at each threshold; plot() draws the decision curve or the \(\Delta NB\) curve of every model; as.data.frame() returns estimates; c() combines results.

summary.voipred_nb(), plot.voipred_nb(), c.voipred_nb(), nb_priors, cipcw_control(), and the value-of-information functions evpi() (with P(useful) and P(best)) and evsi().

The K-value of Wang et al. for two subgroups, from their differences in net benefit (e.g. published values), without patient data: the critical ratio \(k_1/k_2\) of the incremental utility of a true positive relative to a false negative (\(a - c\)) at which population-level net benefit and population utility start to favour different strategies,


\(K = -\frac{n_2 \Delta NB_2}{n_1 \Delta NB_1}.\)
It is defined when the two \(\Delta NB\) have opposite signs. When \(k_1 > k_2\), population net benefit and utility favour different strategies if \(k_1/k_2 > K\); when \(k_1 < k_2\), if \(k_1/k_2 < K\). With patient data, summary() of a result of nb_val() with subgroup gives the same check at every threshold.

k

title: voipred
text:
From one set of draws of the net benefit of every strategy (each model, treat all, treat none), evpi() computes three measures at each threshold: the expected value of perfect information (EVPI, and relative EVPI), the probability that each model is useful, P(useful), and the probability that each strategy is the best, P(best). EVPI is the result itself; P(useful) and P(best) are kept in it, as e$p_useful and e$p_best (for a result e), each with its own print(), summary(), plot() and as.data.frame(). As they come from the same draws, the three measures agree with each other exactly.

evpi(x, ..., n_sim = 1000, labels = NULL)





x


A result of nb_val(), for one model or several.




…


More results of nb_val(), for other models evaluated on the same data, outcome, thresholds and prior (and horizon, cause and censoring), combined as by c(). A result with one model given here with a name is labelled with its name.




n_sim


Number of draws. Default 1000.




labels


Optional names of the models, one per model, in order; default: the models’ labels.



EVPI. The expected loss in net benefit due to uncertainty about which strategy is best. With \(NB_s\) the net benefit of strategy \(s\) and expectations over its posterior:


ENB_{perfect} = E{s NB_s}, ENB{current} = _s E{NB_s},


\(EVPI = ENB_{perfect} - ENB_{current}.\)
EVPI is in net benefit units (net true positives per patient); it is 0 when the best strategy is certain. It is never negative: both terms are means over the same draws.
The relative EVPI compares the gain from perfect information with the gain from using the model(s), both relative to the best default strategy:


rEVPI = {ENB_{current} - {0, E(NB_{all})}}.
For example, 1.25 means that perfect information would give 25% more net benefit than using the best model now. It is Inf when no model is better than the default strategies in expectation (the denominator is 0) and EVPI is positive, and NA when both are 0.
P(useful) (e$p_useful). For each model, the probability that it gives a higher net benefit than both default strategies:


\(P(useful) = P\{NB_{model} > \max(NB_{all}, 0)\} = P(\Delta NB > 0),\)
the share of the draws in which the model’s net benefit is strictly higher. A model that ties with a default strategy (e.g. at a threshold where it treats everyone, or no one) is not counted as useful. P(useful) compares each model only with the default strategies, so it does not depend on the other models.
P(best) (e$p_best). For each strategy, the probability that it has the highest net benefit:


\(P(best_s) = P\{NB_s = \max_t NB_t\},\)
the share of the draws in which it is the best. Exact ties are shared equally, so the probabilities of all strategies add up to 1 at each threshold.

An object of class voipred_evpi, a list with:


estimates: a data frame with one row per threshold and columns threshold, ENB_current, ENB_perfect, EVPI and rEVPI (returned by as.data.frame());


p_useful: P(useful), an object of class voipred_p_useful whose estimates (and as.data.frame()) have one row per threshold and model and columns threshold, model and p_useful;


p_best: P(best), an object of class voipred_p_best whose estimates (and as.data.frame()) have one row per threshold and strategy and columns threshold, strategy and p_best;


ENB: the expected net benefit of each strategy at each threshold;


models, outcome, censoring, prior, draws (“posterior” or “Bayesian bootstrap”), n_sim and call.


The result and its parts have print(), summary(), plot() and as.data.frame() methods (summary.voipred_voi(), plot.voipred_evpi(), plot.voipred_p_useful(), plot.voipred_p_best()); plot(e, type = “p_useful”) and plot(e, type = “p_best”) draw P(useful) and P(best). EVPI can also be drawn under the decision curve with plot(<nb_val result>, evpi = ).

The uncertainty about the net benefit is its posterior (see the prior of nb_val()), represented by n_sim draws, in each of which the net benefit of every model, of treating all and of treating none is computed:


binary outcome: draws from the conjugate posterior of the prevalence and of each model’s sensitivity and specificity, with the prior of nb_val() (exact Beta / Dirichlet draws, as in bayesDCA). Several models are drawn jointly (a Dirichlet over the patterns of treat / do not treat across the models), so their correlation on the same patients is kept, and each model keeps its own posterior;


survival and competing-risks outcomes, and binary outcomes with case weights (improper prior): the Bayesian bootstrap. Each draw gives the patients Dirichlet(1, …, 1) weights (times the case weights) and recomputes the net benefit with the same estimator as nb_val(). With cIPCW (cipcw), the censoring model is refitted in every draw and the censoring weights recomputed from it (see cipcw_control()).


The predicted risks are kept fixed in every draw. The expected net benefits are the means of the draws.

title: voipred
text:
From one set of draws of the net benefit of every strategy (each model, treat all, treat none), evpi() computes three measures at each threshold: the expected value of perfect information (EVPI, and relative EVPI), the probability that each model is useful, P(useful), and the probability that each strategy is the best, P(best). EVPI is the result itself; P(useful) and P(best) are kept in it, as e$p_useful and e$p_best (for a result e), each with its own print(), summary(), plot() and as.data.frame(). As they come from the same draws, the three measures agree with each other exactly.

evpi(x, ..., n_sim = 1000, labels = NULL)





x


A result of nb_val(), for one model or several.




…


More results of nb_val(), for other models evaluated on the same data, outcome, thresholds and prior (and horizon, cause and censoring), combined as by c(). A result with one model given here with a name is labelled with its name.




n_sim


Number of draws. Default 1000.




labels


Optional names of the models, one per model, in order; default: the models’ labels.



EVPI. The expected loss in net benefit due to uncertainty about which strategy is best. With \(NB_s\) the net benefit of strategy \(s\) and expectations over its posterior:


ENB_{perfect} = E{s NB_s}, ENB{current} = _s E{NB_s},


\(EVPI = ENB_{perfect} - ENB_{current}.\)
EVPI is in net benefit units (net true positives per patient); it is 0 when the best strategy is certain. It is never negative: both terms are means over the same draws.
The relative EVPI compares the gain from perfect information with the gain from using the model(s), both relative to the best default strategy:


rEVPI = {ENB_{current} - {0, E(NB_{all})}}.
For example, 1.25 means that perfect information would give 25% more net benefit than using the best model now. It is Inf when no model is better than the default strategies in expectation (the denominator is 0) and EVPI is positive, and NA when both are 0.
P(useful) (e$p_useful). For each model, the probability that it gives a higher net benefit than both default strategies:


\(P(useful) = P\{NB_{model} > \max(NB_{all}, 0)\} = P(\Delta NB > 0),\)
the share of the draws in which the model’s net benefit is strictly higher. A model that ties with a default strategy (e.g. at a threshold where it treats everyone, or no one) is not counted as useful. P(useful) compares each model only with the default strategies, so it does not depend on the other models.
P(best) (e$p_best). For each strategy, the probability that it has the highest net benefit:


\(P(best_s) = P\{NB_s = \max_t NB_t\},\)
the share of the draws in which it is the best. Exact ties are shared equally, so the probabilities of all strategies add up to 1 at each threshold.

An object of class voipred_evpi, a list with:


estimates: a data frame with one row per threshold and columns threshold, ENB_current, ENB_perfect, EVPI and rEVPI (returned by as.data.frame());


p_useful: P(useful), an object of class voipred_p_useful whose estimates (and as.data.frame()) have one row per threshold and model and columns threshold, model and p_useful;


p_best: P(best), an object of class voipred_p_best whose estimates (and as.data.frame()) have one row per threshold and strategy and columns threshold, strategy and p_best;


ENB: the expected net benefit of each strategy at each threshold;


models, outcome, censoring, prior, draws (“posterior” or “Bayesian bootstrap”), n_sim and call.


The result and its parts have print(), summary(), plot() and as.data.frame() methods (summary.voipred_voi(), plot.voipred_evpi(), plot.voipred_p_useful(), plot.voipred_p_best()); plot(e, type = “p_useful”) and plot(e, type = “p_best”) draw P(useful) and P(best). EVPI can also be drawn under the decision curve with plot(<nb_val result>, evpi = ).

The uncertainty about the net benefit is its posterior (see the prior of nb_val()), represented by n_sim draws, in each of which the net benefit of every model, of treating all and of treating none is computed:


binary outcome: draws from the conjugate posterior of the prevalence and of each model’s sensitivity and specificity, with the prior of nb_val() (exact Beta / Dirichlet draws, as in bayesDCA). Several models are drawn jointly (a Dirichlet over the patterns of treat / do not treat across the models), so their correlation on the same patients is kept, and each model keeps its own posterior;


survival and competing-risks outcomes, and binary outcomes with case weights (improper prior): the Bayesian bootstrap. Each draw gives the patients Dirichlet(1, …, 1) weights (times the case weights) and recomputes the net benefit with the same estimator as nb_val(). With cIPCW (cipcw), the censoring model is refitted in every draw and the censoring weights recomputed from it (see cipcw_control()).


The predicted risks are kept fixed in every draw. The expected net benefits are the means of the draws.

Wynants L, Riley RD, Timmerman D, Van Calster B. Random-effects meta-analysis of the clinical utility of tests and prediction models. Statistics in Medicine 2018; 37: 2034-2052. Rubin DB. The Bayesian bootstrap. Annals of Statistics 1981; 9(1): 130-134.

The expected gain in net benefit from a future validation study of size \(N\) (future_n), added to the current sample, before deciding which strategy to use. EVSI is between 0 and EVPI, and approaches EVPI as \(N\) grows: comparing it with the cost of the study helps decide whether more validation data are worth collecting.

evsi(x, ..., future_n, n_sim = 1000, labels = NULL)





x


A result of nb_val(), for one model or several.




…


More results of nb_val(), for other models evaluated on the same data, outcome, thresholds and prior (and horizon, cause and censoring), combined as by c(). A result with one model given here with a name is labelled with its name.




future_n


Sizes of the future validation sample: one or more positive integers.




n_sim


Number of draws. Default 1000.




labels


Optional names of the models, one per model, in order; default: the models’ labels.



For each of n_sim posterior draws (see "Uncertainty"), which define a "true" population with the true net benefit of every strategy, and for each \(N\), a future sample of \(N\) patients is drawn from that population and combined with the current data, the strategy with the highest net benefit in the combined data is chosen, and its true net benefit recorded (Sadatsafavi et al. 2025):


binary outcome: the conjugate algorithm. The future sample is simulated from the draw (events, and the patients treated among them, binomial / multinomial), and the strategy with the highest posterior mean net benefit after updating the posterior with it is chosen;


survival and competing-risks outcomes (and case weights): the bootstrap algorithm. The draw’s Bayesian-bootstrap weights \(W\) define the population; the future sample is \(N\) patients drawn from it (multinomial counts with probabilities \(W\), a future patient being a current patient, with the same follow-up), pooled with the current sample, and the net benefit recomputed with the same estimator as nb_val(). With cIPCW (cipcw) the censoring model is refitted in every draw and every pooled sample (see cipcw_control()).


If strategies tie exactly in the combined data, the mean of their true net benefits is recorded (a random choice among them). Then \(ENB_{sample}\) is the mean of the recorded true net benefits and \(EVSI = ENB_{sample} - ENB_{current}\), with \(ENB_{current}\) as in evpi() (from the same draws). The true EVSI is never negative, but its estimate can be slightly negative where EVPI is close to 0 (Monte Carlo error; more draws make it smaller): read such values as 0.

An object of class voipred_evsi, a list with estimates (a data frame with columns threshold, future_n, EVSI and EVPI, one row per threshold and future sample size), future_n, models, outcome, censoring, prior, draws, n_sim and call. It has print(), summary(), plot() and as.data.frame() methods; EVSI can also be drawn under the decision curve with plot(<nb_val result>, evsi = ).

The uncertainty about the net benefit is its posterior (see the prior of nb_val()), represented by n_sim draws, in each of which the net benefit of every model, of treating all and of treating none is computed:


binary outcome: draws from the conjugate posterior of the prevalence and of each model’s sensitivity and specificity, with the prior of nb_val() (exact Beta / Dirichlet draws, as in bayesDCA). Several models are drawn jointly (a Dirichlet over the patterns of treat / do not treat across the models), so their correlation on the same patients is kept, and each model keeps its own posterior;


survival and competing-risks outcomes, and binary outcomes with case weights (improper prior): the Bayesian bootstrap. Each draw gives the patients Dirichlet(1, …, 1) weights (times the case weights) and recomputes the net benefit with the same estimator as nb_val(). With cIPCW (cipcw), the censoring model is refitted in every draw and the censoring weights recomputed from it (see cipcw_control()).


The predicted risks are kept fixed in every draw. The expected net benefits are the means of the draws.

title: voipred
text:
The expected gain in net benefit from a future validation study of size \(N\) (future_n), added to the current sample, before deciding which strategy to use. EVSI is between 0 and EVPI, and approaches EVPI as \(N\) grows: comparing it with the cost of the study helps decide whether more validation data are worth collecting.

evsi(x, ..., future_n, n_sim = 1000, labels = NULL)





x


A result of nb_val(), for one model or several.




…


More results of nb_val(), for other models evaluated on the same data, outcome, thresholds and prior (and horizon, cause and censoring), combined as by c(). A result with one model given here with a name is labelled with its name.




future_n


Sizes of the future validation sample: one or more positive integers.




n_sim


Number of draws. Default 1000.




labels


Optional names of the models, one per model, in order; default: the models’ labels.



For each of n_sim posterior draws (see "Uncertainty"), which define a "true" population with the true net benefit of every strategy, and for each \(N\), a future sample of \(N\) patients is drawn from that population and combined with the current data, the strategy with the highest net benefit in the combined data is chosen, and its true net benefit recorded (Sadatsafavi et al. 2025):


binary outcome: the conjugate algorithm. The future sample is simulated from the draw (events, and the patients treated among them, binomial / multinomial), and the strategy with the highest posterior mean net benefit after updating the posterior with it is chosen;


survival and competing-risks outcomes (and case weights): the bootstrap algorithm. The draw’s Bayesian-bootstrap weights \(W\) define the population; the future sample is \(N\) patients drawn from it (multinomial counts with probabilities \(W\), a future patient being a current patient, with the same follow-up), pooled with the current sample, and the net benefit recomputed with the same estimator as nb_val(). With cIPCW (cipcw) the censoring model is refitted in every draw and every pooled sample (see cipcw_control()).


If strategies tie exactly in the combined data, the mean of their true net benefits is recorded (a random choice among them). Then \(ENB_{sample}\) is the mean of the recorded true net benefits and \(EVSI = ENB_{sample} - ENB_{current}\), with \(ENB_{current}\) as in evpi() (from the same draws). The true EVSI is never negative, but its estimate can be slightly negative where EVPI is close to 0 (Monte Carlo error; more draws make it smaller): read such values as 0.

An object of class voipred_evsi, a list with estimates (a data frame with columns threshold, future_n, EVSI and EVPI, one row per threshold and future sample size), future_n, models, outcome, censoring, prior, draws, n_sim and call. It has print(), summary(), plot() and as.data.frame() methods; EVSI can also be drawn under the decision curve with plot(<nb_val result>, evsi = ).

The uncertainty about the net benefit is its posterior (see the prior of nb_val()), represented by n_sim draws, in each of which the net benefit of every model, of treating all and of treating none is computed:


binary outcome: draws from the conjugate posterior of the prevalence and of each model’s sensitivity and specificity, with the prior of nb_val() (exact Beta / Dirichlet draws, as in bayesDCA). Several models are drawn jointly (a Dirichlet over the patterns of treat / do not treat across the models), so their correlation on the same patients is kept, and each model keeps its own posterior;


survival and competing-risks outcomes, and binary outcomes with case weights (improper prior): the Bayesian bootstrap. Each draw gives the patients Dirichlet(1, …, 1) weights (times the case weights) and recomputes the net benefit with the same estimator as nb_val(). With cIPCW (cipcw), the censoring model is refitted in every draw and the censoring weights recomputed from it (see cipcw_control()).


The predicted risks are kept fixed in every draw. The expected net benefits are the means of the draws.

Sadatsafavi M, et al. Expected value of sample information calculations for risk prediction model validation. Medical Decision Making 2025; 45(3): 232-244.

row.names, optional


Not used (as in as.data.frame()).



All three have the same layout, for one model or several: one row per threshold and model, the model’s label in the column model, and the columns NB_model, NB_all, NB_none, delta_NB and net_FP_avoided (net false positives avoided against treat all; see nb_val()) (summary() adds Se and Sp). print() and summary() sort the rows by threshold, so that the models are side by side; as.data.frame() keeps the order of the estimates (by model, then threshold).

title: voipred
text:
Conditional inverse probability of censoring weighting (cIPCW) allows censoring to depend on covariates: it assumes censoring is independent of the event time given the covariates of the censoring model. It is used when nb_val() is given cipcw, and most analyses need nothing more than the covariates, cipcw = ~ age + nodes (option 1 below, with the default truncation). cipcw_control() is only needed for the other options: your own censoring model, given weights, another truncation, ties, or your own predict and refit functions.

cipcw_control(
  formula = NULL,
  model = NULL,
  weight_event = NULL,
  weight_horizon = NULL,
  min_prob = 0.02,
  ties = c("left", "right"),
  predict_function = NULL,
  refit_function = NULL
)





formula


Option 1: the covariates of the censoring, a one-sided formula such as ~ age + nodes (variables of data), for a Cox model fitted by voipred. Give one of formula, model or the two weights.




model


Option 2: a survival model fitted to the censoring times of the validation data data passed to nb_val() (same patients), with censoring as the event, e.g. coxph(Surv(time, status == 0) ~ x, data = val).




weight_event, weight_horizon


Option 3: two numeric vectors, one positive finite value per row of data (in its row order), given together: weight_event is the inverse probability of remaining uncensored just before each patient’s own time, 1/G(T_i- X_i), used for patients with an event (of any cause) by the horizon; weight_horizon is the inverse probability of remaining uncensored at the horizon, \(1/\hat G(\tau \mid X_i)\), used for patients event-free at the horizon. Values for the other patients are ignored (any positive number will do). Unstabilized weights only.




min_prob


Truncation, for every option: censoring probabilities below min_prob (options 1 and 2), or weights above 1 / min_prob (option 3), are set to that limit. A single number strictly between 0 and 1; default 0.02 (weights at most 50). NULL: no truncation.




ties


Options 1 and 2, and only matters for a censoring model whose survival curve has steps (e.g. Cox, Kaplan-Meier, forests, trees): “left” (default) uses the probability of remaining uncensored just before each patient’s own time, so a censoring step at exactly that time is not included (the usual convention, as for Kaplan-Meier: an event tied with a censoring comes first); “right” includes it. For smooth (parametric) censoring models both give practically the same result.




predict_function


Option 2, optional: a function(model, newdata, times) returning, for each row of newdata, the probability of remaining uncensored at that row’s time in times (the censoring survival \(G(t \mid X)\), not a risk). It may instead return a curve per row, list(time = <grid>, surv = <n x grid matrix>), which voipred reads at each row’s own time. Use it for a censoring model voipred cannot predict from by itself, or to predict in your own way; it then replaces voipred’s own prediction. Requires model.




refit_function


Option 2, optional: a function(data, weights) returning the censoring model fitted to data (the validation data given to nb_val(), restricted to the patients with a positive weight in a draw) with case weights weights (the Bayesian-bootstrap weights of the draw, positive and averaging 1, times the case weights of nb_val() if any; in evsi() also whole numbers for the pooled samples), e.g. function(data, weights) coxph(Surv(time, status == 0) ~ x, data = data, weights = weights). Used by the value-of-information functions to refit the censoring model in every draw (see "Uncertainty"). Needed for a censoring model voipred cannot refit with case weights by itself.



There are three ways to give the censoring information:
1. The covariates of the censoring (formula =, or simply cipcw = ~ age + nodes in nb_val()). voipred fits a Cox model of the censoring times of the validation data on them, coxph(Surv(time, censored) ~ age + nodes), with only true censoring as the event (with competing risks, patients with a competing event are not censored), weighted by the case weights of nb_val() if any, and refits it in every draw of the value-of-information functions. A two-sided formula (e.g. Surv(time, status == 0) ~ age + nodes) is fitted as it is.
2. A fitted censoring model (model =, or cipcw = <model> in nb_val()). Fit any survival model to the censoring times in the validation data, i.e. with the censored patients as the "events": Surv(time, status == 0). With competing risks, only true censoring is censoring: patients with a competing event are not censored (Surv(time, status == “censored”), not status != cause). voipred predicts from the model the probability of remaining uncensored just before each patient’s own time and at the horizon, in the same way as it predicts risks from a model in nb_val(): through riskRegression::predictRisk() (e.g. coxph with x = TRUE, rms::cph, survreg, flexsurvreg, ranger, randomForestSRC, a Kaplan-Meier prodlim fit), or voipred’s own code for models riskRegression cannot handle (coxph without x = TRUE, aorsf, partykit survival trees, rstpm2::stpm2, mgcv::gam with cox.ph()). For any other model, give predict_function (or the weights, option 3). Where the model’s outcome can be read from its formula, voipred checks it against data: it stops if the model was fitted to the event (for competing risks: to the cause of interest, to another cause or to all events together), and warns if the check is not possible or if the model was fitted to a different number of patients than data has.
3. Weights (weight_event =, weight_horizon =): one value per row of data, the inverse probabilities of remaining uncensored just before each patient’s own time and at the horizon, i.e. \(1/\hat G(T_i- \mid X_i)\) and \(1/\hat G(\tau \mid X_i)\). Only the weights of patients with an event by the horizon (weight_event; including competing events) and of patients event-free at the horizon (weight_horizon) are used. They must be unstabilized: stabilized weights bias this estimator.
Flexible censoring models. A flexible model (e.g. a forest) fitted and evaluated on the same patients overfits their censoring times, and its weights are biased. text:
Conditional inverse probability of censoring weighting (cIPCW) allows censoring to depend on covariates: it assumes censoring is independent of the event time given the covariates of the censoring model. It is used when nb_val() is given cipcw, and most analyses need nothing more than the covariates, cipcw = ~ age + nodes (option 1 below, with the default truncation). cipcw_control() is only needed for the other options: your own censoring model, given weights, another truncation, ties, or your own predict and refit functions.

cipcw_control(
  formula = NULL,
  model = NULL,
  weight_event = NULL,
  weight_horizon = NULL,
  min_prob = 0.02,
  ties = c("left", "right"),
  predict_function = NULL,
  refit_function = NULL
)





formula


Option 1: the covariates of the censoring, a one-sided formula such as ~ age + nodes (variables of data), for a Cox model fitted by voipred. Give one of formula, model or the two weights.




model


Option 2: a survival model fitted to the censoring times of the validation data data passed to nb_val() (same patients), with censoring as the event, e.g. coxph(Surv(time, status == 0) ~ x, data = val).




weight_event, weight_horizon


Option 3: two numeric vectors, one positive finite value per row of data (in its row order), given together: weight_event is the inverse probability of remaining uncensored just before each patient’s own time, 1/G(T_i- X_i), used for patients with an event (of any cause) by the horizon; weight_horizon is the inverse probability of remaining uncensored at the horizon, \(1/\hat G(\tau \mid X_i)\), used for patients event-free at the horizon. Values for the other patients are ignored (any positive number will do). Unstabilized weights only.




min_prob

ties


Options 1 and 2, and only matters for a censoring model whose survival curve has steps (e.g. Cox, Kaplan-Meier, forests, trees): “left” (default) uses the probability of remaining uncensored just before each patient’s own time, so a censoring step at exactly that time is not included (the usual convention, as for Kaplan-Meier: an event tied with a censoring comes first); “right” includes it. text:
The prior of nb_val(). By default nb_val() uses no prior information (nb_improper(): the data only, the usual net benefit); for a binary outcome, prior information can be added with the other priors. The priors are Beta priors on the prevalence of the outcome and, at every threshold, on the sensitivity and the specificity of the model (the probabilities of being treated among patients with the event, and of not being treated among patients without it). The net benefit at threshold \(z\) is


\(NB = \pi \, Se - (1 - \pi)(1 - Sp) \frac{z}{1 - z},\)
and that of treating all \(\pi - (1 - \pi) z / (1 - z)\). The posteriors are Beta distributions (conjugate), so their draws are exact (no MCMC).

nb_beta(prevalence = c(0, 0), sensitivity = c(0, 0), specificity = c(0, 0))

nb_improper()

nb_uniform()

nb_jeffreys()




prevalence, sensitivity, specificity


The two shape parameters \((a, b)\) of each Beta prior, non-negative numbers: prior mean \(a / (a + b)\), worth \(a + b\) patients. Default Beta(0, 0): no prior information, so only the parts you give carry prior information (e.g. nb_beta(prevalence = c(7, 93)) adds information on the prevalence only); nb_beta() is nb_improper().




nb_improper() (default of nb_val()): no prior information. The improper (Haldane) prior, Beta(0, 0) for all three: the data only. The net benefit of nb_val() is then the usual net benefit, \(TP/n - FP/n \cdot z/(1-z)\). It is the only prior for survival and competing-risks outcomes, whose net benefit is the usual Kaplan-Meier, Aalen-Johansen or cIPCW estimate.


nb_uniform(): Beta(1, 1) for all three, as in bayesDCA (binary outcome).


nb_jeffreys(): Jeffreys prior, Beta(1/2, 1/2) for all three.


nb_beta(): Beta priors with the shapes you give, e.g. an informative prior on the prevalence from earlier studies. The priors above are special cases of it.


nb_informative(): the informative prior of bayesDCA, whose sensitivity and specificity priors change with the threshold; for small effective sample sizes (see its help page).


All these priors except nb_informative() are the same at every threshold. For a binary outcome, the result of nb_val() holds the prior shapes used at each of its thresholds (prior_shapes).
With the improper prior, a posterior is degenerate where a count is 0 (e.g. no patient with the event is left untreated at a threshold): it is then the observed proportion, as in the usual net benefit.

A prior, an object of class nb_prior.

The informative prior of bayesDCA (Cruz and Korthauer, 2025), for a binary outcome: Beta priors on the sensitivity and specificity of each model that change with the threshold, and a Beta prior on the prevalence. Give it to nb_val() as prior = nb_informative(); the value-of-information functions then use it too.

nb_informative(
  sensitivity = c(0.99, 0.01),

  ignorance = c(0.25, 0.75),

ignorance_prior

The logic. Under the rule "treat if the predicted risk is at or above the threshold", every model treats everyone at a threshold of 0 (sensitivity 1, specificity 0: treat all) and no one at a threshold above all predicted risks (sensitivity 0, specificity 1: treat none). Near the ends of the decision curve few patients are untreated (low thresholds) or treated (high thresholds), so the data say little there, and a vague prior lets the net benefit, and the value-of-information measures, swing widely. This prior states, with little weight, that the model behaves like treat all at the lowest threshold and like treat none at the highest, and stays vague in between. Cruz and Korthauer (2025) found that such a prior keeps EVPI decreasing with the sample size in small samples, where it otherwise may not.

The priors at different thresholds are independent; each model has the same prior. The prevalence has the Beta prior prevalence at every threshold.

title: voipred
text:
voipred (the R package voipred.dev) evaluates clinical prediction models in a validation sample by their clinical utility, and quantifies how much the remaining uncertainty matters for the decision of whether to use them.

Net benefit and decision curves (nb_val()), for binary, survival and competing-risk outcomes, for one model or several compared on the same patients; with Kaplan-Meier or conditional inverse probability of censoring weights (cIPCW) for informative censoring.
Value of information analysis: the expected value of perfect information (EVPI), the probability that each model is useful and that each strategy is the best (evpi()), and the expected value of sample information of a further validation study (evsi()).
A Bayesian framework, which by default gives the usual net benefit, with optional prior information, including the informative prior of bayesDCA (nb_informative()).



# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("amirfarahmand0/voipred_dev")



The article Introduction to voipred walks through a complete analysis: net benefit and decision curves, comparing models, value of information, prior information, survival and competing-risk outcomes, and reporting. The Reference (in the menu) documents every function.
